message: Review case file C14, 'Case file C14: Border farmland, a legacy minefield and a strip near a recent clash site'. The parts of the area are A: the farmland nearest the village; B: the minefield at the foot of the ridge; C: the strip along the ridge road, near the 2025 clash site. The evidence log holds items E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, E6, E7, E8. Recommend an outcome for a person to sign off.

result.text:
## 1. Area record

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Area ID | THA-SHA-1402 |
| Country | Thailand, on the border with Cambodia |
| Setting | Farmland and scrub in a border district, below a ridge along a stretch of the border that is not demarcated. A minefield from the conflicts of the 1980s and 1990s runs along the foot of the ridge. Armed clashes took place nearby in 2025, and the military has closed the ridge road since. |
| Recorded status | Suspected hazardous area (SHA), from an impact survey in 2001; the minefield at the foot of the ridge was confirmed by technical survey in 2019 |
| Suspected hazard | Anti-personnel mines |
| Parts | A: the farmland nearest the village; B: the minefield at the foot of the ridge; C: the strip along the ridge road, near the 2025 clash site |
| Survey | Non-technical survey by an accredited survey team of the national mine action centre, with a female team member, 10–12 August 2026 |
| Field visit | Completed, except part C |
| Parts not reached | C: closed by the military since the 2025 clashes |
| Community meeting | Held |
| Groups consulted | Men; women (in a separate meeting); the village head; farmers who work part A |

## 2. How the area was recorded
An impact survey in 2001 recorded the area as suspected, from villagers' reports of a minefield at the foot of the ridge. In 2019 technical survey confirmed mines there, defined the edge of the minefield and marked it; the farmland lies outside that edge. After armed clashes near the ridge road in 2025, the military closed the road, and the survey team could not enter the strip along it.

## 3. Evidence log

| ID | Evidence | Source | Location | Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | The 2001 impact survey recorded the whole area as suspected, from villagers' reports of a minefield at the foot of the ridge; it gives no boundary. | National database, 2001 impact survey record | Whole area | 2001 |
| E2 | Technical survey in 2019 found mines at the foot of the ridge, defined the edge of the minefield, and marked it with posts and signs; the report places the farmland outside that edge. | National database: technical survey report | Part B; the edge between parts A and B | 2019 |
| E3 | A farmer was injured by a mine at the foot of the ridge in 2012, at a spot that his son, who was with him, showed the team. | National casualty database; the farmer's son | Part B, at a known spot | 2012 |
| E4 | "I have grown cassava on this land every year since 2004. We plough it with a tractor, and nothing has ever been found." | Farmer who works part A himself | Part A | Interview, 11 August 2026 |
| E5 | The women said they plant, weed and harvest the fields every season and collect firewood along the field edges, and have never seen anything suspicious. | Women's meeting (10 women), held separately | Part A | Meeting, 11 August 2026 |
| E6 | The national authorities reported that soldiers were injured by mines near the border in 2025, and attributed the mines to new laying by the neighbouring country's forces. The neighbouring government denied laying new mines and said the explosions were in old minefields. No independent fact-finding had confirmed either account by the time of the survey. | Statements by the two governments, as reported in the press | Part C; exact places not given | 2025 |
| E7 | The military closed the ridge road and the strip along it after the 2025 clashes; the team could not enter, and villagers have not used the strip since. | Survey team; village head | Part C | 11 August 2026 |
| E8 | The team walked the field edges and the marked edge of the minefield, and saw no items in the farmland; the posts and signs of 2019 are in place. | Survey team observation | Part A; the edge of part B | 11 August 2026 |

## 4. Community meeting
Held at the village temple on 11 August 2026. The men (12) and the women (10) met separately; the female team member led the women's meeting. The village head and the farmers who work part A took part. Everyone knows where the marked minefield is and keeps out of it. Since the 2025 clashes, nobody goes up to the ridge road.

## 5. Land use
Years of safe use count the whole years of use with no finds and no accidents.

| Part | Use | Since | Years of safe use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Cassava, ploughed by tractor every year | 2004 | 22 |
| B | Not used; marked minefield | — | 0 |
| C | Not used since the road was closed in 2025; before that, a footpath beside the road | — | Unknown |

## 6. Survey team remarks
The farmland has been used safely for more than twenty years and lies outside the minefield that technical survey defined in 2019. The minefield at the foot of the ridge is confirmed. The team could not enter the strip along the ridge road. Given the reports of new mines laid by the neighbouring country's forces, the team recommends clearance of the whole area, including the strip, as soon as the military allows.

## 7. National criteria box

| Criterion | National rule (invented) |
|---|---|
| Cancellation by non-technical survey | Allowed |
| Minimum years of safe use to cancel | 5 |
| First-hand sources needed to confirm safe use | 2 |
| Groups that must be consulted before cancellation | Men; women |
| Correction of duplicate or wrong records by desk review | Allowed, with a technical survey report, completion report or handover certificate |
| Clearance without technical survey | Allowed where direct evidence defines the hazard |
| Other rules | Areas that the survey team cannot reach for security reasons are recorded as not surveyed, and returned for survey when access allows. Claims about who laid mines are recorded with their source; they do not decide the outcome. |

## 8. Attachments
The 2019 technical survey report and its sketch (not reproduced here). Six photographs of the farmland and the marked minefield (not reproduced here).

## Direct and indirect evidence
- Direct evidence is verifiable information that confirms with certainty that EO is present. Indirect evidence suggests that EO may be present but does not confirm it (IMAS 07.11, §3.5, §3.10).
- Indirect evidence supports an SHA and needs checking by technical survey before any decision to clear. Direct evidence supports a CHA and leads to technical survey or clearance (IMAS 07.11, §4.4).
- All information is assessed for credibility, reliability and relevance, and is traceable to its source (IMAS 07.11, §4.4).
- Examples of indirect evidence (IMAS 08.10, §6.1): productive land left unused; verbal reports from local people, former combatants and others; records whose reliability is doubtful or has not been assessed; analysis of tactics, nearby known areas and history; former combat zones; earlier surveys not backed by direct evidence; accidents whose location cannot be determined accurately.
- Examples of direct evidence (IMAS 08.10, §6.1): records shown to be reliable in earlier operations; EO, parts of EO or fragments seen; detonations during fires or caused by animals; mine signs, fencing or equipment associated with contamination; accidents whose location can be determined accurately.
- Craters: IMAS 08.10 (§6.1) lists craters seen among the examples of direct evidence, but the newer IMAS 07.11 (2026, §4.3) gives "visible craters" as an example of indirect evidence. This project follows the newer standard unless the case's national criteria say otherwise.
- Bombing and artillery records and unit diaries are not direct evidence of cluster munition remnants, although they help to plan survey (TNMA 08.20/02, §8.1).
- Project rule: an item moved from where it was found (for example, brought to a scrap yard or a house) is not evidence about the place where it now lies.
- Project rule: marking or fencing put up only as a precaution, because an area was suspected, is not direct evidence on its own: it shows the suspicion, and is worth what the suspicion rests on. Marking put up because of a known minefield, finds or accidents is direct evidence (IMAS 08.10, §6.1).
- Project rule: statements that attribute explosive ordnance to a party are recorded as the claims of their source. The reviewer takes no side in them; what matters is what the evidence shows about where explosive ordnance is.
- Project rule: evidence about a place outside the area under review is recorded with the part "outside". It can explain evidence inside the area (for example, a record that places a minefield elsewhere), but it is not evidence of EO inside the area.

## Suspected and confirmed hazardous areas
- A suspected hazardous area (SHA) is an area with reasonable suspicion of explosive ordnance (EO) on the basis of indirect evidence. A confirmed hazardous area (CHA) is one where EO has been confirmed by direct evidence (IMAS 07.11, §3.4, §3.19).
- Decisions rest on evidence, "not the lack thereof". An area with no indirect or direct evidence is not recorded as an SHA or CHA; areas with only indirect evidence are SHAs; areas with direct evidence should be CHAs (IMAS 07.11, §4.2).
- Fear alone does not make a hazardous area. People may avoid land out of fear, but fear has to be backed by evidence (IMAS 07.11, §4.2).
- Areas that are inaccessible, or about which little is known, are not recorded as SHAs or CHAs by default (IMAS 07.11, §4.2).
- Low impact on a community is never on its own a reason to cancel an area; it may lower the area's priority (IMAS 07.11, §4.2).
- A single item found outside an SHA or CHA is an EOD spot task, recorded as a point rather than an area, unless further survey shows wider contamination (IMAS 07.11, §3.9, §4.5).
- CHA boundaries are drawn around the places where the direct evidence is; nearby land with only indirect evidence may be an SHA (IMAS 07.11, §4.5).

## When land can be cancelled
- Cancelled land is an SHA or CHA concluded not to contain evidence of EO, on reliable information that meets set cancellation criteria (IMAS 07.11, §3.2).
- Where no evidence was found, release criteria are met only if the efforts made could reasonably have been expected to find evidence of any contamination (IMAS 07.11, §4.3).
- Cancellation through non-technical survey requires that all reasonable effort has been applied, and that it can be shown with high confidence that there is no evidence of EO in the area. Absence of evidence counts only if the efforts made could reasonably have found evidence, had contamination been present (IMAS 08.10, §6.2).
- Recommendations to cancel existing areas are made only when all reasonable effort has been applied (IMAS 08.10, §7).
- Wrong, duplicate or redundant records may be amended, merged or removed, but only on documented and verifiable evidence (IMAS 07.11, §8.2).
- Not reasons to cancel: low impact alone (IMAS 07.11, §4.2); great effort in one respect that leaves gaps in others (IMAS 08.10, §6.3).
- Project rule: protected habitat, or the cost of survey, may limit the methods used, but is not a reason to cancel.
- Communities, including women, girls, boys and men, are consulted closely on decisions to cancel, reduce or hand over land (IMAS 07.11, §11.2).
- If direct evidence is later found on cancelled land, the land is reclassified as a CHA (IMAS 07.11, §10).

## Land and road use
- The use of land or a road may be weighed when assessing information, or when considering cancelling all or part of an area (IMAS 08.10, §8.3).
- Weigh it systematically: the contamination known nearby; exactly which land is used and which is not; how it is used, including how deep any digging or ploughing goes and how dense and intensive the traffic is; and for how long, including whether the use changed over time (IMAS 08.10, §8.3).
- An area recorded as an SHA on indirect evidence may later be cancelled if there is evidence of safe human activity over time, such as several years of farming (IMAS 07.11, §4.3).
- Parts of an area with different usage histories should be defined as separate zones (IMAS 08.10, §8.3). Hazardous areas should be subdivided where the type of contamination, the confidence in the evidence or the suitable methods differ (IMAS 08.10, §8.4).

## Returning a case for more non-technical survey
- Where too little information was collected for a confident decision, managers should consider whether more non-technical or technical work would provide it (IMAS 08.10, §7).
- SHAs and CHAs are not defined because information is lacking, but only on indirect or direct evidence (IMAS 08.10, §7; IMAS 07.11, §4.2).
- Where so little is known that TS cannot be targeted, more non-technical effort is generally needed (IMAS 08.20, Introduction).
- Project rule: a case goes back for more non-technical survey when the field visit or the community meeting is missing, when groups that the national criteria require were not consulted, or when the evidence is too thin to target TS.

## The outcomes the reviewer may recommend (project rule)
The reviewer recommends one outcome for the whole area, or a split that gives each part of the area its own outcome:
- `CANCEL`: release by non-technical survey, because all reasonable effort found no evidence of EO (IMAS 07.11, §3.2; IMAS 08.10, §6.2).
- `TECHNICAL_SURVEY`: targeted technical survey, to confirm or rule out contamination and to reduce the area (IMAS 08.20, §5.3), including CMRS for cluster munition remnants.
- `CLEARANCE`: clearance of a confirmed hazardous area (IMAS 07.11, §3.3 and §4.4).
- `FURTHER_NTS`: the case goes back to the survey team for more non-technical survey before any decision (IMAS 08.10, §7).
- `SPLIT`: each part of the area (A, B, ...) is named once, with its own outcome, where the parts differ in use, evidence or confidence (IMAS 08.10, §8.3 and §8.4).

Every recommendation is tested by the rule check and signed off by a person. The reviewer never makes the final decision.

## All reasonable effort
- All reasonable effort is the minimum acceptable level of effort. It has been applied when committing more resources would be unreasonable compared with the results expected. The national authority defines it (IMAS 07.11, §3.1 and §3.12).
- Before land is cancelled, reduced or cleared, it should be established with high confidence that there is no longer any evidence of EO (IMAS 07.11, §5).
- It includes identifying and reaching all relevant sources of information, including women, girls, boys and men, and historical material; suitable activities and procedures; and communication, so that stakeholders understand and accept the process (IMAS 07.11, §5).
- Survey should reach both male and female informants, with separate meetings where some groups might not speak freely in mixed ones (IMAS 08.10, §8.1).
- Great effort in one respect does not make up for too little in others (IMAS 08.10, §6.3).

## 7. National criteria box

| Criterion | National rule (invented) |
|---|---|
| Cancellation by non-technical survey | Allowed |
| Minimum years of safe use to cancel | 5 |
| First-hand sources needed to confirm safe use | 2 |
| Groups that must be consulted before cancellation | Men; women |
| Correction of duplicate or wrong records by desk review | Allowed, with a technical survey report, completion report or handover certificate |
| Clearance without technical survey | Allowed where direct evidence defines the hazard |
| Other rules | Areas that the survey team cannot reach for security reasons are recorded as not surveyed, and returned for survey when access allows. Claims about who laid mines are recorded with their source; they do not decide the outcome. |

arguments.summary: Recommend split release. Cancel A: it lies outside the minefield boundary defined by the 2019 technical survey, and the farmer and women provide separate first-hand accounts of 22 years of safe, intensive use, meeting the national cancellation criteria and addressing the broad 2001 suspicion for this part. Recommend clearance of B: mines were confirmed there, its boundary was defined, and national criteria allow clearance without another technical survey where direct evidence defines the hazard. Return C for further non-technical survey when access is permitted; the team could not reach it, while conflicting 2025 reports suggest possible hazard but give no exact locations. Do not infer absence from its non-use or inaccessibility.
arguments.guidance: Keep people and animals away from the marked minefield and the military-closed ridge-road strip. Do not touch, move or try to destroy any suspected item. Mark a place only if this can be done without going closer, and report it to the authorities. Use A only in accordance with the authority's signed-off release decision.
flags: Part C was not surveyed because of military security restrictions; national criteria require it to be recorded as not surveyed and returned when access allows.
The 2025 claims about who laid mines are disputed and unverified; record the claims with their sources and do not treat attribution as deciding the outcome.
The survey team's recommendation to clear the whole area is evidence for review, not a decision; this recommendation differs for A and C based on the evidence and national criteria.
